subject: Finding bad items - itemfit in multidimensional graded model

messages.author: e2cb1c0fedcc0ea5
messages.subject: Finding bad items - itemfit in multidimensional graded model
parts:
Hi,

I am doing a 6-dimensional exploratory mirt analysis with 45 likert-scaled variables and n=550. I want to delete variables in order to improve my total variance explained(~30%). First I did like I would do in factor analysis and deleted items based on loadings and h2. I deleted around 10 items and the total variance explained was around 50% and it was easy to tell why the items had been bad in almost every case. But then I stumbled across a post in which Chalmers said h2 is arbitrary in mirt, and realized I should use itemfit(). But according to Kang & Chen (2011), S_X2 doesn't really work with an n this small and with this many items. Also, I couldn't explain why S_X2 and Zh flagged the items they had flagged and had not flagged items I knew should be bad. How should I decide which items to delete?

Also, both itemfit() and M2() functions work without imputing missing values, but then the values aren't stable (they change a bit every time you ran the functions again). Does this mean I have to impute missing values or is it ok to estimate these values based on unimputed values? I have <6% missing per variable. Here is an example of what I have done:

fscores <- fscores(mirt_un, method = "MAP", full.scores = TRUE, rotate = "oblimin")
imputed <- imputeMissing(mirt_un, scores)
Warning message:
In is.na(data) : is.na() applied to non-(list or vector) of type 'closure' ## Is this a problem?
(mirt_imputed<- mirt(imputed, 6, itemtype = 'graded', method = 'MHRM', QMC = TRUE))
itemfit(mirt_imputed, c('S_X2', 'Zh'), QMC = TRUE)
M2(mirt_imputed, impute=10, QMC = TRUE)

Thank you in advance! With kind regards,

Erica


Article referenced: Kang, T., & Chen, T. T. (2011). Performance of the generalized SX 2 item fit index for the graded response model. Asia Pacific Education Review, 12(1), 89-96.

On Mon, Mar 26, 2018 at 9:46 AM, Erica Michelsson <ericami...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi,

I am doing a 6-dimensional exploratory mirt analysis with 45 likert-scaled variables and n=550. I want to delete variables in order to improve my total variance explained(~30%). First I did like I would do in factor analysis and deleted items based on loadings and h2. I deleted around 10 items and the total variance explained was around 50% and it was easy to tell why the items had been bad in almost every case. But then I stumbled across a post in which Chalmers said h2 is arbitrary in mirt,

That may have been a different context. Sometimes, items with low loadings may still be useful (e.g., in early CAT applications), but if your strategy is to implement some type of revised/short form then this strategy is not terrible.

and realized I should use itemfit(). But according to Kang & Chen (2011), S_X2 doesn't really work with an n this small and with this many items. Also, I couldn't explain why S_X2 and Zh flagged the items they had flagged and had not flagged items I knew should be bad. How should I decide which items to delete?

Hard to say, and depends on "how bad" these items violate their fit. If the misfit is marginal then the response functions may still be useful as an approximate whole, but this gets into robustness versus prestince filtering arguments.

Also, both itemfit() and M2() functions work without imputing missing values, but then the values aren't stable (they change a bit every time you ran the functions again). Does this mean I have to impute missing values or is it ok to estimate these values based on unimputed values? I have <6% missing per variable.
The imputed approach used here shouldn't be relied on too seriously as it does make conservative results. Missing data problems really do make these types of analyses difficult.

Here is an example of what I have done:

fscores <- fscores(mirt_un, method = "MAP", full.scores = TRUE, rotate = "oblimin")
imputed <- imputeMissing(mirt_un, scores)
Warning message:
In is.na(data) : is.na() applied to non-(list or vector) of type 'closure' ## Is this a problem?
This could be a problem. Could you provide a reproducible example (can be emailed privately)?
(mirt_imputed<- mirt(imputed, 6, itemtype = 'graded', method = 'MHRM', QMC = TRUE))

I would not re-estimate the model with the imputed parameters, that's bound to make the model even more conservative. Use the above code, but supply the previous models parameters to pars=mod2values(prev_model), and pass TOL = NaN to ensure the model is not estimated.

itemfit(mirt_imputed, c('S_X2', 'Zh'), QMC = TRUE)
M2(mirt_imputed, impute=10, QMC = TRUE)

Thank you in advance! With kind regards,

Erica


Article referenced: Kang, T., & Chen, T. T. (2011). Performance of the generalized SX 2 item fit index for the graded response model. Asia Pacific Education Review, 12(1), 89-96.

messages.author: 67ad43f188b9c5e7
messages.subject: Re: Finding bad items - itemfit in multidimensional graded model
parts:
Hi Erica,

I have a similar question as you posted, wherein I have n=600 and <4% missing data for each variable.
Also, both itemfit() and M2() functions work without imputing missing values, but then the values aren't stable (they change a bit every time you ran the functions again).

I wonder what you you mean by "the results are stable without imputation". In my case, the codes did not work (there is error warning) with missing value; so I have to create a dataset with complete cases (i.e. no missing at all); and results from the imputed model and the complete case model are different (specially, model fit M2 statisticsand itemfit probability, but the parameters and factor loadings are pretty comparable). 

Also, in term of item-level diagnostics, I have talked to a psychometrician in UNC and he suggested look at the LD table FIRST; if that helps. 

Best,
Yingyi

Thank you very much for your answer! And this group & mirt :D

I sent you some data via email and some commands I tried. I was unable to get the command to work with the suggested modification.

> (mirt_TS_imp <- mirt(TS_imp, 6, pars=mod2values(mirt1), TOL = NaN, itemtype = 'graded', method = 'MHRM', QMC = TRUE))
Stage 3 = 1, LL = -26541.2, AR(0.39) = [0.13], gam = 0.0000, Max-Change = 0.0000Error in if (all(abs(gamma * correction) < TOL)) conv <- conv + 1L else conv <- 0L : 
  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

Btw have you thought about adding Tarkkonen's reliability to the mirt package? It is an excellent measure to estimate reliability, albeit hasn't had much attention yet. Here some articles about it:

Vehkalahti, K., Puntanen, S., & Tarkkonen, L. (2006). Estimation of reliability: a better alternative for Cronbach's alpha. Helsinki: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of Helsinki.

Vehkalahti, K., Puntanen, S., & Tarkkonen, L. (2009). Implications of dimensionality on measurement reliability. In Statistical inference, econometric analysis and matrix algebra(pp. 143-160). Physica-Verlag HD.


With kind regards and deeply thankful,
Erica
